text: Lessons 4 and 5 built and tested a REST Message entirely from the record, without a line of script anywhere. This lesson finally calls it from script, using the real ServiceNow API built for exactly that job: RESTMessageV2.

In a scoped application you reference it as sn_ws dot RESTMessageV2; in Global scope, you can drop the namespace prefix and just use RESTMessageV2 directly, since both point at the same underlying API. The constructor takes exactly two strings: the REST Message's name and the specific Function's name you configured back in Lessons 4 and 5. Get either one wrong — a typo, a renamed record — and you're pointed at the wrong configuration, or none at all.

Remember the Function's Endpoint from Lesson 4 — slash current, question mark, city equals a placeholder. That placeholder doesn't fill itself in on its own. Script calls setStringParameterNoEscape, once per placeholder the Function defines, with the placeholder's name as the first argument and the real value as the second. Three placeholders in a Function means three separate calls, all before execute ever runs.

Execute sends the configured request synchronously and returns a response object once it completes. getStatusCode, called on that response object, returns the real HTTP status code — the exact same kind of value you watched on the Test screen last lesson, just now available to script instead of a human reading a form. getBody returns the raw response as a string, typically JSON, ready for JSON.parse to pull individual fields out of.

Here's the distinction that actually matters: a 500 returned by the external system is still a successful execute call, as far as JavaScript itself is concerned — your status-code check in an if statement handles that case cleanly. But a real network-level failure, like DNS not resolving or a connection timing out, makes execute throw a genuine exception instead of returning anything at all. That's exactly why execute belongs inside a try/catch — a network failure shouldn't be allowed to stop your script cold with no explanation.

Constructor names the operation, setStringParameterNoEscape fills in placeholders, execute sends it, try/catch catches what execute itself can't recover from. Next up: the full lab, assembling all of this into a real WeatherAPI integration end to end.
